title: Anabaptists
hookLine: Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites: adult baptism, simplicity and nonviolence, at great cost

lines: HE SAVES THE MAN CHASING HIM.
cards: The Netherlands, winter, 1569. Dirk Willems has escaped from prison, where he's been held for his faith, and he's running across a frozen pond, a guard chasing him.
Dirk makes it across; the ice holds his thin, starved body. Behind him, the guard crashes through and starts to drown, screaming for help. Dirk is free.
Nobody would blame him for running. He stops. He turns around.

He goes back across the ice and pulls his pursuer out. The guard wants to let him go, the story says, but the magistrate on the shore orders him taken. Dirk is led back to prison, and soon after he's burned at the stake.

teach.b: Anabaptists means rebaptizers, from the Greek ana, again. Their enemies gave them the name.
They said they weren't baptizing anyone again: the baptism of a baby, before it could believe, simply wasn't baptism in their eyes.
It began in Zurich in January 1525, when a small group met in a house and Conrad Grebel baptized a former priest, George Blaurock, as an adult who had chosen to follow Christ. It was dangerous.
Catholic and Protestant authorities alike treated infant baptism as the glue of society. Within two years, one of that group, Felix Manz, was drowned in Zurich's river.
Many more were executed in the decades that followed. From them come families still living today. The Mennonites, named for Menno Simons, a Dutch former priest.
The Amish, who split from the Mennonites in the 1690s under Jakob Ammann. The Hutterites, who hold all property in common.

They differ, but share a few things: baptism for believers who choose it; a church separate from the state; simplicity; and nonviolence, taken straight from the Sermon on the Mount: "resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also."

teach.h: TURN TO HIM THE OTHER ALSO.
teach.b: Many refuse military service, even at great cost. It's why the Amish choose carefully which technology to let in: not because machines are evil, but to protect the life of the community.
And it's why a man running for his life turned back on the ice.

how: Anabaptist churches baptize those old enough to choose faith, many refuse military service, and communities such as the Amish and Hutterites live simply, share work, and decide together which modern tools to use.

o: Christians who think one baptism can't cover all sins
people who reject baptism and every other sacrament
people who baptize only believers old enough to choose

s: Anabaptists chose the name for themselves
it means rebaptizers, and their enemies gave it to them.
the Amish avoid some technology because they think machines are evil
they choose carefully to protect the life of the community.
the first adult baptism of the movement was in Zurich in 1525

games.q: you've escaped prison and made it across the ice. behind you, the guard chasing you has fallen through and is drowning. what do you do?
o: go back and pull him out.
shout for someone else to help.
games.why: Dirk Willems went back and saved him. he was taken again, and soon after burned at the stake. his story is still read in Amish and Mennonite homes.

practice: Picture one simple hour, later today or tomorrow: no screen, no buying, maybe a walk, a slow meal, a conversation, work with your hands. See it clearly, and notice how much quieter it feels.
If you pray, offer that hour to God; if not, let it be an hour of peace, for you and anyone near you.

wordCard.voice: Anabaptists. The rebaptizers, a name from their enemies: Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites, who baptize believers and choose simplicity and peace.

orig.note: Greek: to dip or immerse. With ana, again, it gave the name rebaptizers.

carryVoice: Your line: the peaceable way. Chosen baptism, a simple life, and the other cheek. Peace to you.
